name: Laser-cut acrylic
spec: Cast acrylic, typically 10 mm, flame-polished edge, matte or gloss face
why: The default for lettering that has to look sharp for a decade. Laser cutting leaves a clear polished edge that catches light along every stroke, which is what makes the letters read as objects rather than stickers. Matte faces are the safer choice under downlights — a gloss face directly below a spotlight becomes a mirror.
fire: Combustible. Standard cast acrylic is not fire resistant, so where a specification calls for a rated material we quote PVC foam or aluminium instead — or a flame-retardant acrylic grade, which exists but costs more and is worth ordering only when the rating is actually required.

name: Mirror acrylic
spec: 3 mm mirror acrylic in gold, silver or black, flame-polished edge
why: A mirror face reflects the room rather than holding a colour of its own, which is why a set of it changes character between a window wall and a corridor. Lighter and far safer than glass mirror — it will not shatter, so it belongs where glass is not allowed, and it takes a polished edge that reads as a finished object rather than a cut sheet. Wipe with a soft cloth only; a gritty cloth is the one thing that marks it.
fire: Combustible, like all acrylic. Its advantage over glass mirror is breakage, not fire: it will not shatter into edges. Where a rating is required, the same piece can be cut in polished aluminium instead.

name: PVC foam board
spec: Expanded PVC, typically 19 mm, sprayed satin, sealed edge
why: Light enough to mount with tape alone on a wall that cannot be drilled, and unaffected by humidity — it will not swell or warp the way a timber letter can. The 19 mm depth is what makes a shadow read from across a room; anything under 10 mm looks applied rather than mounted.
fire: The best fire performer here, and the reason it is the default for schools and corridors. Expanded PVC is self-extinguishing — chlorine makes up over half its mass and acts as a flame retardant, giving it a limiting oxygen index of 35–45%, so it stops burning once the flame source is removed. Thin gauges reach Class A under ASTM E84. Ask and we will send the supplier's test data for the exact sheet.
bestFor: Schools, universities, corridors, leased offices, cafés

name: CNC-routed MDF
spec: MDF, typically 19 mm, primed and sprayed to any colour, sealed faces
why: The most economical route to a large word cloud, and the only one that takes an exact brand colour without a premium. Sealed on every face so the cut edge cannot draw moisture. Kept away from wet areas, where PVC is the correct answer instead.
fire: Standard MDF is Class D — combustible, with a long flame-spread. Fire-retardant MDF reaching Class B is available and is what we quote for an escape route or anywhere a rating is specified; it costs more, so it is worth asking for only where it is needed.
fireShort: Class D; FR grade reaches Class B

name: Brushed aluminium
spec: 3 mm aluminium face on 15 mm returns, clear anodised
why: For reception and lobby walls that appear in photographs of the company. The brushed grain reads as a material rather than a colour and does not date. Longest-lived of these and the most forgiving of being cleaned around.
fire: Non-combustible. Where a specification leaves no room — an atrium, a protected stairwell, a hospital corridor — this is the material that answers it without a conversation.
bestFor: Reception walls, lobbies, atriums, stairwells, meeting-room fronts

name: 3D-printed PLA
spec: Continuous-line print, typically 8 mm depth, colour through the material
why: The only practical way to make continuous outline work — a single unbroken line that a cutter cannot produce. The colour is the filament rather than a coat of paint, so there is no finish to chip. Light enough for tape mounting, which keeps a leased wall intact.
fire: Combustible, with no useful rating. Fine on an office or classroom wall; not what we would put on an escape route, where PVC foam or aluminium is the right answer.
